title: Rental Income Is Three Different Numbers and Only One of Them Qualifies the Borrower: AI on the Investment-Property Calculation
summary: A lease says one number, the appraiser's Form 1007 says another, and Schedule E says a third, and an underwriter has to pick the right one under rules that change by occupancy and by how long the borrower has owned the property. How an AI agent produces an auditable rental-income figure under Fannie Mae B3-3.1-08, where the 75 percent factor applies, and the reasonableness call the underwriter still owns.
body_markdown:
## Why Rental Income Breaks Automation That Handles W-2s Fine


A salaried borrower's income is close to a solved problem for a document reader: find the paystub, find the W-2, confirm they agree, apply the continuity rules. Rental income is not that, and lenders that automated the W-2 case cleanly still route every investment-property file to a human, because the rental calculation is three different numbers depending on which document you read and which of several rules applies to this specific borrower and this specific property.


I own the income agents on our origination side, and rental is the income type where the math has to be shown rather than asserted. The reason is that the inputs disagree with each other by design. A current lease states the actual rent. The appraiser's comparable-rent schedule, Form 1007 for a single unit or Form 1025 for two-to-four units, states market rent. The borrower's tax return, Schedule E, states what the property actually netted after expenses last year. These are three legitimate numbers and they are rarely the same, and the rule that decides which one qualifies the borrower turns on facts an underwriter has to establish before any arithmetic happens. An agent that picks a number without establishing those facts is not saving anyone time. It is manufacturing a defect.


## What the Rule Actually Says, and the Part Everyone Misremembers


The governing text is[Fannie Mae Selling Guide B3-3.1-08, Rental Income](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-3.1-08/rental-income) . Start with eligibility, because the most common rental error happens before any arithmetic: using income the guide does not let you use. Rental income qualifies only when it is likely to continue, and the guide draws hard lines on source. Income from a one-to-four-unit investment property qualifies, and so does income from the non-occupied units of a two-to-four-unit property the borrower lives in. Income from the borrower's own principal residence or a second home generally does not qualify, with narrow exceptions for boarder income and for an accessory unit. An agent that pulls rent off a borrower's primary-residence basement and adds it to qualifying income has produced a number that fails on eligibility before the factor is ever applied.


Then the factor, which is the part people misremember as a flat haircut. When the calculation uses a lease or the market rent from Form 1007 or Form 1025, the lender multiplies the gross monthly rent by 75 percent and then subtracts the full monthly housing expense for that property, the principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and any HOA dues. The 25 percent that comes off is not a buffer the lender invented. It stands in for vacancy and maintenance, and it is why the number that qualifies the borrower is almost never the rent on the lease. The result can be negative, and when it is, the shortfall is a liability in the debt-to-income ratio rather than income. A reader that reports the gross rent as income, or that forgets to net the housing expense, overstates the borrower's capacity in the direction that gets a lender a repurchase.


Schedule E runs on a different path. When the property has a rental history, the calculation starts from the net income or loss the borrower reported, adds back the non-cash and non-recurring items the guide allows, depreciation, insurance, mortgage interest, taxes, and HOA dues among them, and adjusts for the number of months the property was in service. The guide and its net-rental-income worksheets, Form 1038 for an established history and Form 1039 for a property not on the prior return, exist precisely because this is a multi-step calculation where the add-backs are specific and a missed one changes the answer. Short-term rentals get a heavier reduction than the standard 25 percent, because the income is less stable, which is one more case where the factor is not a single constant.


## How the Agent Produces a Number an Auditor Can Follow


The agent does not pick a number. It runs every applicable path, shows each one, and selects the one the rule requires for this file, with the reason. On a newly acquired investment property with no rental history on the tax return, the path is the lease and the Form 1007 market rent, and the agent takes the figure the guide directs for that case, applies the 75 percent factor, subtracts the full housing expense from the Loan Graph, and reports the net. On a property the borrower has owned and reported on Schedule E, the agent runs the Schedule E path, pulls each add-back line by line from the return, adjusts for months in service, and reconciles it against the current lease to check the income has not fallen off a cliff since the return was filed. Where both a history and a current lease exist, the agent follows the guide on which governs rather than averaging them, because averaging is not a method the rule recognizes.


The output is not a single figure. It is the figure plus the worked path, every input cited to the document and line it came from: the lease to its executed page, the market rent to the Form 1007 grid, each Schedule E add-back to its line on the return, the housing expense to the Loan Graph fields that feed the full PITIA. An underwriter reading the file sees the number and the arithmetic that produced it in one view, which is the difference between a figure they have to re-derive to trust and one they can confirm. The same view is what an investor's QC reviewer or an examiner reads later, so the calculation is auditable at origination rather than reconstructed under a repurchase demand.


## The Governance That Has to Sit Around It


An income figure feeds the debt-to-income ratio, which feeds the ability-to-repay determination, so the component that produces it is a model in the credit path and we govern it as one under[SR 11-7](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/sr1107.htm) . That means the rental calculator is validated against a labeled set of real investment-property files before it runs live, with the labels set by underwriters, and it means the error we monitor is the confident wrong number on a file the agent cleared without help, not the headline share of files it handled alone. The direction of the error matters as much as its rate. An agent that understates rental income is conservative and costs the borrower a loan they might have qualified for. An agent that overstates it puts a loan on the books the borrower cannot carry, which is the error the ability-to-repay rule exists to prevent. So the thresholds are set so that overstatement is the error the agent escalates first.


## Where the Underwriter Still Signs


The reasonableness call is the underwriter's, and the agent is built to bring that call to them rather than make it. The guide's continuity test, whether the income is likely to continue, is a judgment, not a lookup. A lease that runs month-to-month, a tenant who is a family member, a rent well above the appraiser's market figure, a Schedule E showing a loss every year the borrower has owned the property: these are facts the agent surfaces and does not resolve. It stops and routes the file with the specific question named and the conflicting documents attached. A market rent on Form 1007 that sits far from the lease is not a number the agent silently splits. It is a discrepancy it hands to the underwriter, because the gap usually means something the file has not yet explained.


The agent also stops when the documents do not support any clean path: a Schedule E that references a property the appraisal does not match, a lease with no executed signature, a return that is a draft rather than a filed copy backed by a transcript. The most frequent real-world outcome on a rental file is a missing or inconsistent document rather than a hard calculation, and the agent's job there is to go get the right document rather than compute on a bad one.


What the agent takes off the underwriter's desk is the part that is pure, error-prone arithmetic: pulling the add-backs without missing one, applying the right factor for the occupancy and the rental type, netting the housing expense, and doing it the same way every time. The part it leaves on the desk is the judgment the rule assigns to a person, brought to them with the math already done and cited. At Sei we run rental as one calculation inside the income desk rather than a special case handled offline, because the figure belongs in the Evidence Trail next to the rest of the file, and the loan officer who used to lose a day to a Schedule E gets the file back with the number worked and the open question, if there is one, named at the top.
